n8-licao-rbac.enunciado:
Every action in the cluster is a request to the API (“list pods in the loja namespace”), and RBAC decides whether whoever asked is allowed. There are four pieces:

  • Role: a type of badge inside one namespace. A list of rules: these verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete) on these resources (pods, pods/log, deployments...).
  • ClusterRole: the same, valid across the whole cluster (or reused in several namespaces). Some come ready-made: view (read only, except Secrets), edit, admin and cluster-admin.
  • RoleBinding: hands a badge (Role or ClusterRole) to someone, inside one namespace.
  • ClusterRoleBinding: hands out a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.

“Someone” is a user (User), a group (Group) or a ServiceAccount: the machine badge that pods use to talk to the API (spec.serviceAccountName; if you don’t set it, it’s default).

Ask before you try

kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=ana -n loja          # no
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:loja:painel -n loja

--as asks “as if I were” someone else (you, the admin, are allowed to). Without permission, the answer is a Forbidden that says exactly what was missing:

Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "ana" cannot list resource "pods"
in API group "" in the namespace "default"

The catch: a RoleBinding that points to a ClusterRole is valid only in the RoleBinding’s namespace. To make it valid in all of them, use a ClusterRoleBinding.
n8-licao-rbac.vidaReal: Everyone in the condo has a badge. The badge type (Role) says which doors it opens; the handover (RoleBinding) says who got which badge.
n8-licao-rbac.limite: Badges only add up: there’s no “can do everything except delete.” To deny something, just don’t grant it.

n8-quem-apaga.enunciado: In the loja namespace, ana, bruno and carla have different badges. Only one of them can delete pods there. Who?
n8-quem-apaga.dica: kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=NAME -n loja, for each of them.
n8-quem-apaga.vidaReal: Three employees, three badges. Before sending someone to fix the problem, find out who has the right key.
n8-quem-apaga.limite: can-i answers by the rules, not by intent: if someone was given more than they should have, it still says “yes.”

testes.descricao: you found who has the key

n8-cracha-de-leitura.enunciado:
Give ana, only in the loja namespace, permission to read pods and their logs (get, list and watch on pods and pods/log). No deleting.

The file already has the leitor Role, but with one verb too many. Fix it and hand over the badge (RoleBinding).
n8-cracha-de-leitura.dica: Remove delete from the Role and add a RoleBinding (subjects: kind User, name ana; roleRef: kind Role, name leitor).
n8-cracha-de-leitura.vidaReal: ana will keep an eye on the store: she needs to see the apartments and read each one’s diary, without touching anything.
n8-cracha-de-leitura.limite: Reading logs can expose sensitive data: a read-only badge needs care too.
n8-cracha-de-leitura.comoSaber: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=ana -n loja says yes; with delete, no.

n8-cracha-pelo-terminal.enunciado: From the terminal, in the loja namespace: create the atualizador Role (get, list, create and update on deployments) and hand it to bruno with the bruno-atualizador RoleBinding.
n8-cracha-pelo-terminal.dica: kubectl create role atualizador --verb=get,list,create,update --resource=deployments -n loja and kubectl create rolebinding bruno-atualizador --role=atualizador --user=bruno -n loja
n8-cracha-pelo-terminal.vidaReal: bruno handles the store’s updates: viewing, creating and updating Deployments. The management office issues the badge on the spot, over the counter.
n8-cracha-pelo-terminal.limite: create role doesn’t check whether the resource makes sense for the job: you’re the one who picks the bare minimum.
n8-cracha-pelo-terminal.comoSaber: kubectl auth can-i update deployments --as=bruno -n loja says yes.

n8-conta-do-painel.enunciado:
The painel pod uses the painel ServiceAccount, which doesn’t exist: the apply is rejected.

In the same file, before the pod, create the painel ServiceAccount, a ver-pods Role (get, list and watch on pods) and a painel-ver-pods RoleBinding that hands the Role to the ServiceAccount.
n8-conta-do-painel.dica: In the RoleBinding’s subjects: kind: ServiceAccount, name: painel, namespace: default.
n8-conta-do-painel.vidaReal: The front gate’s panel is a machine: it needs a badge of its own (like the elevator’s, or the cameras’), one that opens only what it uses.
n8-conta-do-painel.limite: Every pod has a badge, even if it’s just “default.” Giving permissions to default gives them to every pod in the namespace.
n8-conta-do-painel.comoSaber: The pod comes up, and kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:painel says yes.

testes.descricao: painel comes up and sees only pods

n8-auditoria.enunciado:
The auditoria (auditor) user should be able to read (the view ClusterRole) in every namespace, but the badge was handed over with a RoleBinding in default: in kube-system she sees nothing.

Replace it with a ClusterRoleBinding.
n8-auditoria.dica: kind: ClusterRoleBinding, with no namespace in metadata.
n8-auditoria.vidaReal: The auditor needs to look at every block of the condo without touching anything. The badge was handed over only at one block’s front gate.
n8-auditoria.limite: view doesn’t show Secrets: even the auditor needs a separate badge to read passwords (and should almost never have one).
n8-auditoria.comoSaber: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=auditoria -n kube-system says yes.

testes.descricao: auditoria reads in every namespace, without touching anything

n8-licao-netpol.enunciado:
By default, every pod talks to every pod, in any namespace. A NetworkPolicy picks pods (podSelector) and, from then on, only lets through what it allows:

  • ingress: who they accept connections from (from) and on which ports.
  • egress: who they can talk to (to).
  • The peers in from/to: podSelector (pods in the same namespace), namespaceSelector (pods in other namespaces, by the namespace’s label, such as kubernetes.io/metadata.name) or ipBlock.
# deny all ingress to the pods in the namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress

Rules add up: a pod picked by two policies accepts whatever either of them allows. Watch out for ingress: [{}]: an empty rule allows everything.

The DNS catch

Closed a pod’s outbound traffic (egress)? It stops talking to DNS (kube-dns, port 53, UDP and TCP) and no name resolves: wget: bad address 'api'. Open port 53 to kube-dns along with it.

The policies are enforced by the network plugin (CNI). kindnet enforces them; some plugins don’t, and then the policy is just decoration.
n8-licao-netpol.vidaReal: Without inner turnstiles, any visitor who got into the condo can walk through every block. NetworkPolicy installs turnstiles and says who gets through.
n8-licao-netpol.limite: With no policy at all, everything stays open: you need a “deny all” rule to close things off, and then you open what’s needed.

n8-nega-tudo.enunciado:
In the rede namespace, right now any pod can call api. The file has a nega-tudo (deny-all) policy that should block incoming traffic to all pods in the namespace, but it blocks nothing.

Fix it.
n8-nega-tudo.dica: “ingress: [{}]” is a rule that allows everything. With no ingress rule at all, nothing gets in.
n8-nega-tudo.vidaReal: A block’s first turnstile is the one that shuts everything: after that, you open what’s needed.
n8-nega-tudo.limite: It only closes the way in: the pods in there can still go out wherever they want (for that, an Egress policy).
n8-nega-tudo.comoSaber: From inside curioso, kubectl exec curioso -n rede -- wget -q -O- -T 3 http://api gives download timed out.

n8-so-a-vitrine.enunciado: The rede namespace has nega-tudo in place. Allow traffic into api only from app=vitrine pods. The file already has the policy, but vitrine is still blocked.
n8-so-a-vitrine.dica: The rule’s port is the one on the receiving container (nginx listens on 80), not some other one.
n8-so-a-vitrine.vidaReal: The api’s block is closed. The vitrine pod (the storefront) needs a turnstile pass; curioso (the nosy one) doesn’t.
n8-so-a-vitrine.limite: The turnstile trusts the label: any pod with the label app=vitrine gets through too. Who can set labels is a matter of RBAC.
n8-so-a-vitrine.comoSaber: The vitrine pod gets the nginx page; curioso gets download timed out.

n8-dns.enunciado:
The saida-da-vitrine policy lets vitrine talk only to api, on port 80. But from inside it, wget http://api gives bad address 'api'.

Add an egress rule for DNS: the k8s-app=kube-dns pods in the kube-system namespace, port 53, UDP and TCP.
n8-dns.dica: A second item in egress, with to: [{ namespaceSelector: {...kube-system}, podSelector: {...kube-dns} }] and the two 53 ports.
n8-dns.vidaReal: They allowed vitrine to talk only to api, and forgot that, to find api, it asks the switchboard operator (DNS) for the address.
n8-dns.limite: Using the IP directly, vitrine would reach api: the only thing blocked was the name lookup.
n8-dns.comoSaber: kubectl exec vitrine -n rede -- wget -q -O- -T 3 http://api shows the nginx page.

msgs.2: the rest of the exit stays closed (kube-dns port 9153 times out)

n8-outro-bloco.titulo: The neighbor from the other block
n8-outro-bloco.enunciado:
The rede namespace is closed off (nega-tudo). The coletor pod, in the monitoramento namespace, needs to call api. The policy in the file uses only a podSelector, which looks for pods in its own namespace, rede.

Replace it with a namespaceSelector for the monitoramento namespace.
n8-outro-bloco.vidaReal: The metrics collector lives in another block (the monitoramento namespace). The api’s turnstile needs to recognize whoever comes from there.
n8-outro-bloco.limite: Allowing a whole namespace allows any pod created there later, too. Combine it with a podSelector to tighten it.
n8-outro-bloco.comoSaber: kubectl exec coletor -n monitoramento -- wget -q -O- -T 3 http://api.rede shows the nginx page.

n8-licao-seguranca.enunciado:
By default, the program in most images runs as root inside the container. If it gets hacked, the attacker starts out with the master key. The securityContext (on the pod or on each container) tightens this:

  • runAsUser: 1000: runs as a regular user. runAsNonRoot: true: refuses to start as root (CreateContainerConfigError: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root).
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true: the container’s disk becomes read-only; the program writes only to volumes (an emptyDir where it needs one).
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }: no gaining power after it starts.
  • seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }: the default filter for system calls.

Pod Security Admission

The fire marshals of each block: a label on the namespace picks the standard and the mode.

kubectl label ns cofre pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
  • Standards: privileged (no rules), baseline (no privileged, hostNetwork, hostPath...) and restricted (baseline plus the securityContext above).
  • Modes: enforce rejects the pod, warn only warns.

The catch: a Deployment in a restricted namespace is created with a Warning, but its pods are rejected. The symptom is READY 0/1, and the reason is in kubectl describe rs (FailedCreate).
n8-licao-seguranca.vidaReal: Nobody gets the master key: each resident runs with the key to their own apartment. And the fire marshals (Pod Security) don’t let in anyone who asks for more than they should.
n8-licao-seguranca.limite: The standards look at what the pod asks for, not at what the program does: a buggy program is still buggy, just with less power.

n8-sem-root.enunciado: Make the relatorio (report) pod run as user 1000 (runAsUser) and refuse to start as root (runAsNonRoot), in the pod’s securityContext.
n8-sem-root.vidaReal: The report runs with the condo’s master key for no reason. Give it a regular resident’s key.
n8-sem-root.limite: Running as a regular user doesn’t protect the data the program already reads: it only limits the damage if it gets hacked.

msgs.1: the id inside the container is 1000

n8-somente-leitura.enunciado:
vitrine (nginx) got readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and went into CrashLoopBackOff. Check the reason in the logs (kubectl logs deploy/vitrine).

Without removing read-only, give nginx two emptyDir volumes: at /var/cache/nginx and at /var/run.
n8-somente-leitura.dica: volumes: [{ name: cache, emptyDir: {} }, { name: run, emptyDir: {} }] and the volumeMounts in the container.
n8-somente-leitura.vidaReal: They sealed the apartment’s walls (nobody writes on them), but nginx needs a desk to work at and a spot for the day’s badge.
n8-somente-leitura.limite: Whatever the program writes to the emptyDir is gone when the pod leaves: it’s just the work desk.
n8-somente-leitura.comoSaber: The vitrine pod becomes ready, with its disk still read-only.

testes.descricao: vitrine starts with a read-only disk

n8-normas-dos-bombeiros.enunciado:
The cofre (safe) namespace has pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. The guarda (guard) Deployment gets created, but stays at 0/1: its pods are rejected (kubectl describe rs -n cofre tells you what’s missing).

Adjust the pod’s and the container’s securityContext until guarda comes up.
n8-normas-dos-bombeiros.dica: On the pod: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. On the container: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"].
n8-normas-dos-bombeiros.vidaReal: The safe’s block follows the strictest fire code. The guard was hired, but the front gate won’t let him in the way he showed up.
n8-normas-dos-bombeiros.limite: Passing the standard doesn’t make the program secure: it only ensures it starts without powers it doesn’t need.

testes.descricao: the guard got into the safe
the safety locks are still there

msgs.0: the cofre namespace still has the restricted standard: tearing up the fire code doesn’t make the guard any safer
